title: Fixed-Schedule Productivity
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. borrows Cal Newport's concept of fixed-schedule productivity: commit in advance to how much work you will do, then optimize inside that limit. He reports keeping his own rule of no work after 5:30 and none on weekends, and argues that his output comes because of the constraint, not despite it. Following Newport, he gives two reasons it works, namely that it forces prioritization and that it forces conscientiousness. The teaching application is concrete: leave bulletin boards alone, check email once or twice a day, and grade quickly and purposefully since papers cannot go home. The move is to defend sustainable teacher workload as a productivity strategy backed by an outside authority.
points: Fixed-schedule productivity starts from a firm commitment on how much you will work, and productivity follows from the limit.
The constraint forces prioritization, so a teacher separates work that promotes long-term flourishing from work that does not.
Stuart gives up bulletin-board polish, limits email to once or twice daily, and grades efficiently to protect the work that matters.
The constraint also forces conscientiousness: with no taking papers home, grading and planning must be done purposefully within the day.
Starting with constraints is presented as a Newport-backed principle, not just folksy wisdom.
quotes: In Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World, Newport introduces a concept that he calls fixed-schedule productivity — to optimize your productivity, begin with a commitment for how much work you'll do. Newport's commitment is the same as mine: I don't work after 5:30, and I don't work weekends.
what we would both agree on is that our productivity isn't despite the fixed-schedule commitments we keep, but because of them.

First, fixed-schedule productivity (FSP) forces prioritization. Newport categorizes work as deep or shallow; as a teacher, I might categorize it as stuff that's most likely to promote long-term flourishing and stuff that's not.

For me as a teacher, I've learned to largely leave my bulletin boards alone (I try, and often fail, to keep an updated word wall, but that's it — there are yellow posters on my board that used to be white), to do email one to two times per day, and to grade efficiently and purposefully.

When taking the papers home to grade them isn't an option, I have to get grading done as quickly and purposefully as possible. I can't grade AoWs for four minutes apiece because I wouldn't possibly be able to then plan lessons or read like a professional.
In other words, starting with the constraints isn't just a Dave Stuart Jr. folksy-wisdom thing; it's a Cal Newport productivity guru deep thinker thing.
